sections.title: Quantifiers and pronouns with singular or plural verbs
sections.content:
With any of, each of, either of, neither of, or none of and a plural noun / pronoun we can use a singular or plural verb. (We use a singular verb in formal written English.)
• I don't think any of them knows (or know) where the money is hidden.
With a / the majority of, a number of, a lot of, plenty of, all (of), or some (of) and a plural noun / pronoun we use a plural verb. (We use a singular verb with the number of.)
• A number of refugees have been turned back at the border.
• The number of books in the library has risen to over five million.
After one of and a plural noun / pronoun we use a singular verb. However, after one of + plural noun / pronoun + who we can often use either a singular or plural verb. (A plural verb is more formal.)
• He's one of those teachers who insist / insists on pupils sitting silently in class.
With any of, none of, the majority of, a lot of, plenty of, all (of), some (of) and an uncountable noun we use a singular verb.
• All the furniture was destroyed in the fire.
With every or each and a singular noun or noun phrase with and, we use a singular verb.
• Every boy and girl takes part in the activity.
With everyone, everybody, everything (and similar words beginning any-, some- and no-) we use a singular verb.
• Practically everyone thinks that Phil should be given the job.

sections.title: Joined by and
sections.content:
When a subject has two or more items joined by and, we usually use a plural verb:
• Ingrid and Tobias are moving back to Australia.
However, phrases connected by and can also be followed by singular verbs if we think of them as making up a single item:
• The lorry, its cargo and passengers weighs around 35 tonnes. (or ... weigh ...)

sections.title: Joined by (either) ... or ... / (neither) ... nor ...
sections.content:
When a subject is made up of two or more items joined by (either) ... or ... or (neither) ... nor ... we use a singular verb if the last item is singular (although a plural verb is sometimes used in informal English), and a plural verb if the last item is plural:
• Either the station or the cinema is a good place to meet. (or ... are ... in informal English)
• The President or his representatives are to attend the meeting.
If the last item is singular and previous item plural, we can use a singular or plural verb:
• Either the teachers or the principal is to blame for the accident. (or ... are to blame ...)

sections.title: There + be / have
sections.content:
In there + be / have we use a singular verb form with singular and uncountable nouns and a plural form with plural nouns. However, in informal speech we often use a shortened singular form of be or have (= There's) with plural nouns:
• Over the last few years there have been many improvements in car safety.
• There's been lots of good films on lately. (or There've been ...)

exercises.question: I'd be surprised if any of my children ___ my birthday.
exercises.hint: With 'any of' + plural noun, we can use a plural or singular verb (singular is more formal).
exercises.explanation:
Answer: remember / remembers
With 'any of' + plural noun, we can use a plural or singular verb (singular is more formal).

exercises.sentence: The majority of the work have already been completed.
exercises.correction: The majority of the work has already been completed.
acceptable: The majority of the work has already been completed.
exercises.hint: 'The majority of' + uncountable noun → singular verb.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: The majority of the work has been completed
'The majority of' + uncountable noun takes a singular verb (because the noun is uncountable). With a countable plural noun, the verb is usually plural: 'The majority of students were happy'. But with uncountable nouns (work, information, money), use singular.

exercises.question: It is estimated that the number of ___ of the flooding ___ 100,000.
exercises.hint: Use 'the number of' + plural noun + singular verb.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: victims ... exceeds
Use 'the number of' + plural noun + singular verb.

exercises.sentence: Every student and teacher in the school are affected by the new rules.
exercises.correction: Every student and teacher in the school is affected by the new rules.
acceptable: Every student and teacher in the school is affected
exercises.hint: 'Every + noun + and + noun' is grammatically singular.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: Every student and teacher is affected
Despite 'and' joining two nouns, 'every + noun + and + every + noun' (or simply 'every A and B') takes a SINGULAR verb. 'Every' forces singularity. Similarly: 'Each student and teacher is responsible'. Compare: 'The students AND teachers are affected' (no 'every' = plural).

exercises.question: Plenty of jobs ___ available, but no one ___ them because they're so poorly paid.
exercises.hint: 'Plenty of' + plural noun takes a plural verb. 'No one' takes a singular verb.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: are ... wants
'Plenty of' + plural noun takes a plural verb. 'No one' takes a singular verb.

exercises.sentence: Not only the students but also the teacher were surprised.
exercises.correction: Not only the students but also the teacher was surprised.
acceptable: but also the teacher was surprised
exercises.hint: With 'not only...but also', the verb agrees with the nearest subject ('teacher' = singular).
exercises.explanation:
Answer: the teacher was surprised
'Not only...but also' follows the proximity rule: the verb agrees with the subject nearest to it. Here, 'the teacher' (singular) is nearest to the verb 'was'. If the order were reversed ('Not only the teacher but also the students'), the verb would be 'were'.

exercises.question: The majority of those questioned ___ that the government's economic policies have failed.
exercises.hint: 'The majority of' + plural noun takes a plural verb.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: think
'The majority of' + plural noun takes a plural verb.

exercises.question: Professor Smith and Dr Peters ___ that the wreck of the ship and its cargo ___ a danger to local people fishing near the island.
exercises.hint: Two items joined by 'and' take a plural verb ('claim'). A compound subject thought of as a single unit ('wreck and its cargo') can take a singular or plural verb.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: claim ... constitutes / constitute
Two items joined by 'and' take a plural verb ('claim'). A compound subject thought of as a single unit ('wreck and its cargo') can take a singular or plural verb.
